title: Dasharatha's death and the curse that caused it (Shravana Kumara)

segments.voice: Yesterday: shabdavedhi, an archer who shoots at sound. The young prince shot at a sound in the dark and found a young ascetic with a water pot.

The young man in the river doesn't curse Dasharatha. That's the first surprise. He's dying, and what he talks about is his parents. They're old, and both blind, sitting in a hut nearby, thirsty, waiting for me to bring water. Go to them. Tell them. Then he asks one more thing: pull out the arrow. It's burning. The prince knows that if he pulls it, the boy will die. He does it anyway, because he was asked.
screen: `HE DOESN'T CURSE THE PRINCE.` → `MY PARENTS ARE BLIND AND THIRSTY.` → `PULL OUT THE ARROW.`

segments.voice: So Dasharatha fills the pot and walks the path the boy described. At the hut, the old father hears footsteps and speaks first. Why are you so late, son? Your mother was worried. Did we upset you? Say something. Picture the prince standing there with the water, mistaken for the son he has just killed. This is the moment the episode turns on. Nobody saw. He could set the pot down and slip away. Instead he tells them everything: who he is, the sound, the elephant he imagined, the arrow. In Valmiki's telling, the father answers with something striking. Because you told us yourself, you are still alive. Had you hidden it, far worse would have followed. The confession doesn't undo the death, but it changes what follows. The parents ask to be taken to their son. They sit with his body by the river, touching his face, grieving aloud. Then the father speaks the words that will shape Dasharatha's life. Just as I am losing my life in grief for my son, you too will one day die grieving for a son. And the old couple give up their lives on their son's funeral fire. Hold both halves. Telling the truth spared the young prince that night. It didn't spare him the curse. And tonight, with Rama gone and his own life fading, the old king tells Kausalya the curse is coming true.
screen: `WHY ARE YOU SO LATE, SON?` · `HE COULD SLIP AWAY. HE TELLS THEM.` · `YOU TOLD US YOURSELF.` · `YOU TOO WILL GRIEVE FOR A SON.` · then, large: `THE CURSE, COMING TRUE.`

segments.voice: Think of something small you once got wrong and never quite said out loud, something you can hold gently. Picture telling it plainly to the person it touched, nothing added, nothing hidden, and notice how it feels just to imagine saying it straight.
Dasharatha's death and the curse that caused it. The blind father's words: as I die grieving for my son, you too will die grieving for a son.

howItsDone: This episode is often told on its own as a story about duty to parents, and about a prince who told a blind couple the truth instead of slipping away.

original.note: Sanskrit śāpa: a curse. the king tells this one as a curse he knows is coming true.

trapdoor: what you thought: the boy's family wants revenge.
what it means: the father's curse is grief speaking: you will lose a son as I have.
what a scholar hears: the father credits the confession with sparing the prince's life; had he hidden it, the father says, far worse would have followed.

chat.says: If nobody saw, why did the prince tell the blind parents what he'd done?
options: He chose truth, and the father said that confession is why he still lived.
He thought the parents had already heard the cry and knew what he'd done.
He hoped that if he confessed, the father would not curse him at all.
chat.meaning: Dasharatha could have slipped away. He told them everything, and the father said the confession spared his life, though not the curse.

Valmiki.meaning: the poet-sage who composed the Ramayana

Rama.meaning: prince of Ayodhya, hero of the Ramayana

notes: Sarga numbers follow the vulgate numbering; confirm.
In Valmiki the boy also tells the prince he need not fear the sin of killing a Brahmin, giving his parents' birth. The script leaves this out; a Keeper may want it addressed.
The father's line about the confession sparing the prince (in some versions his head would have split) is paraphrased softly; confirm.
Some versions have the son appear in a heavenly form to his parents before they die; omitted here.
